definition: Interactive machine translation (IMT), is a specific sub-field of computer-aided translation.
details: Under this translation paradigm, the computer software that assists the human translator attempts to predict the text the user is going to input by taking into account all the information it has available. Whenever such prediction is wrong and the user provides feedback to the system, a new prediction is performed considering the new information available. Such process is repeated until the translation provided matches the user's expectations. Interactive machine translation is specially interesting when translating texts in domains where it is not admissible to output a translation containing errors, hence requiring a human user to amend the translations provided by the system. In such cases, interactive machine translation has been proved to provide benefit to potential users. Nevertheless, there are few commercial software that implements interactive machine translation and work done in the field is mostly restrained to academic research.

explainer.lead: Interactive machine translation is a sub-field of computer-aided translation in which the software predicts the text the human translator will type. It matters because it keeps the human in control while accelerating the translation cycle.

tiers.eli5: It is like a typing assistant that guesses your next words, learns from your corrections, and keeps guessing until the sentence matches what you meant.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers build IMT systems that predict the translator's input from all available information and re-predict whenever the user corrects a wrong guess. A common pitfall is that the loop only converges if feedback is fed back into the prediction promptly and accurately.
tiers.paperLevel: In IMT, the assisting software predicts the user's upcoming text from available information; when a prediction is wrong and the user gives feedback, a new prediction is made with the new information, repeating until the translation matches the user's expectations.

explainer.example: A translator accepts a predicted phrase, then edits one word; the system discards the stale prediction and regenerates the remainder of the sentence from the corrected prefix.
